```{r}
install.packages("pwr")

library(pwr)
library(tidyverse)

load(file = "Demo Data Files/CleanOwlLimpet_Data2023.Rdata")
```

## 1. The Setting: Owl Limpet T-test

So in our Owl Limpet Analysis assignment, we ran a t-test and found that there was a [highly]{.underline} significant difference (p \< 0.0000000000000001, *LOL*) in limpet shell size between Corona del Mar and Treasure Cove.

```{r}
t.test(CDM_Data2022$shell_length_mm, TC_Data2023$shell_length_mm)
```

```{r}
ggplot(All_Size_Data) + 
  aes(x = shell_length_mm, color = site) + 
  geom_density()
  
```

## 2. Hypothesis Testing Review

For any given statistical test, there are some default hypotheses.

- $H_0$: The **null hypothesis** is usually that [there is no relationship]{.underline} between the variables, or no difference in means between treatments/samples.

- $H_A$: The **alternative hypothesis** is that [there is a relationship]{.underline} between the tested variables, or a difference in means between treatments/samples.

In our owl limpet study, the null is that there is no difference in mean owl limpet shell length between CDM and TC, and the alternative is that there is a significant difference in means. Significant in this case does not just mean "large" or "notable"; **statistical significance** is defined as a determination made by an analyst that **the results in the data are not explainable by chance** alone.

What makes this different from just eyeballing is that with statistics, you are measuring the relationship between the variables while also **quantifying exactly how certain or uncertain** you are that the relationship you have found is correct. We are only able to take random samples that we hope are representative of the true relationships that exist in nature; the larger the sample, the more likely we are to detect a true relationship.

All the possible outcomes of any statistical test are summarized in the table below:

+---------------------+--------------------------------------+---------------------------------------+
| Null Hypothesis is: | TRUE                                 | FALSE                                 |
+=====================+======================================+=======================================+
| REJECTED            | ***Type I error: "False positive"*** | "True positive"                       |
|                     |                                      |                                       |
|                     | ***Probability = α***                | Probability = 1 - β                   |
+---------------------+--------------------------------------+---------------------------------------+
| NOT REJECTED        | "True negative"                      | ***Type II Error: "False negative"*** |
|                     |                                      |                                       |
|                     | Probability = 1 - α                  | ***Probability = β***                 |
+---------------------+--------------------------------------+---------------------------------------+

: Table 1: Types of error in hypothesis testing

The bold column headers represent the true, unknowable relationship; on the rows is our conclusion about the null hypothesis. When we find a significant result, we say that "We reject the null hypothesis". We will explore the quantities α and β more below.

## 3. Components of a Power Analysis

- Effect size (Cohen's d, or ES) - difference between the means divided by the pooled standard deviation
  - How big is the difference?
- Sample Size (n)
  - How many did you have to count?
- Significance level (Type I error probability, or α)
  - What are the odds that if you decided there is a difference, that you're wrong?
- Power of test (1 - β, alternately written as 1 - Type II error probability)
  - What are the odds that if you decide that there is no difference, that you're right?

The formulas differ a little depending on the statistical test you're running and are not especially pretty, but you can use functions in R to calculate any of these metrics as long as you have the other three.

The basic relationship is:

$$Power ∝ (ES × α × √n)/σ$$

That is, **power** is proportional to **effect size** times **significance** times the **square root of the sample size**, all divided by the **pooled standard deviation**. You can think of the proportional symbol like a wobbly equals sign (=); if you alter the quantities on one side, the other will change too, but the exact values/calculations depend on what kind of statistical test you're applying it to (e.g., t-test, ANOVA, etc.).

We can intuit from this equation how certain quantities will change with each other.

### Effect Size

Effect size is a quantitative measure of the magnitude of the experimental effect. The larger the effect size the stronger the relationship between two variables. For a test of difference, this can be a larger difference between means. For a correlation or regression, this can be how "tight" the relationship is.

```{r}
var1 <- rnorm(10, mean = 12, sd = 1)
var2 <- rnorm(10, mean = 5, sd = 1)
var3 <- rnorm(10, mean = 11, sd = 1)
large <- c(var1,var2)
small <- c(var1,var3)

names <- c(rep("var1", 10), rep("var2", 10))
diff_large <- tibble(names, large)
diff_small <- tibble(names, small)

large <- ggplot(diff_large, aes(names,large)) + geom_boxplot() + labs(title = "large effect size", x = "", y = "")
small <- ggplot(diff_small, aes(names,small)) + geom_boxplot() + labs(title = "small effect size", x = "", y = "")

tight <- tibble(sort(var1), sort(var3))

loose <- ggplot(tight, aes(var1,var3)) + geom_point() + geom_smooth(method = "lm") + labs(x = "", y = "")
tightlm <- ggplot(tight, aes(`sort(var1)`,`sort(var3)`)) + geom_point() + geom_smooth(method = "lm") + labs(x = "", y = "")

install.packages("patchwork")
library(patchwork)

(small | large) / (loose | tightlm)
```

#### Intuiting Effect Size

How do you determine an appropriate effect size? A good rule of thumb if you have no idea comes from Cohen (1988), who famously suggested a rough rule of thumb that an absolute value of d=0.2 was a "small" effect, d=0.5 was a "medium" effect, and d=0.8 was a "large" effect. Across many fields, d = 0.8 is conventionally accepted and standard. However, deciding what a practically important effect size would be really depends on the question you're asking and the system that you're working in.

Consider the two scenarios:

- You are testing a new herbicide to control invasive plants, and find that it kills 5% more invasive plants than the old herbicide (p \<0.05).

  - How much more effective would the herbicide need to be for it to be worth it to switch brands?

- You need to know if the new herbicide is safe for the native plants you are trying to conserve, and find that it kills 5% more of the endangered native plants than the one that you were using before (p \< 0.05).

  - How much more lethal does it need to be before you get concerned?

In the first scenario, a small effect size was hardly worth mentioning, but in the other, you take notice because the stakes are higher. Notice how the statistical significance (the p-value) had nothing to do with how [practically important]{.underline} the results were.

#### Calculating Effect Size

So what was our **effect size** for the difference in limpet shell size between TC and CDM?

$$(μ_1 - μ_2)/σ_{12}$$

$$(mean_1 - mean_2) / stdev_{pooled12}$$

```{r}
# what was our effect size for the difference between CDM and TC? 
mean_CDM <- mean(CDM_Data2022$shell_length_mm)
mean_TC <- mean(TC_Data2023$shell_length_mm)
pooled_sd <- sd(All_Size_Data$shell_length_mm)

Effect_size <- abs(mean_CDM - mean_TC)/pooled_sd

print(Effect_size)
```

We may not have needed to collect QUITE that many samples.

### Sample Size

Experiments with higher sample sizes are able to detect smaller differences (i.e., effect sizes) with more confidence (i.e., lower p-value). If you have a very large sample size, it's common to get a statistically significant result from a test, simply because you can detect ever smaller effect sizes.

However, larger sample sizes in ecological experiments can be a lot of work, space, and expense, all of which may be limited, especially in conservation projects. What was our sample size at Treasure Cove?

```{r}
# sample size at each location within TC
install.packages("janitor")

location_n_TC <- All_Size_Data |>
  group_by(site) |>
  count() |>
  janitor::adorn_totals("row")
  
knitr::kable(location_n_TC)
```

Remember, the number of experimental units (all the observations in the whole study) is not the same as the sample size (the number of replicates for each treatment). Having roughly equal sample sizes across treatments makes for easier statistical analysis.

It took 25 people over two hours this year, plus 15 people over two hours at CDM last year to collect data on 439 limpets. That's a lot, and we already saw that our effect size was gigantic.

Therefore, you may be motivated to find out the minimum sample size you need in order to detect an practically important (i.e., effect size) and significant (confident) difference.

#### Estimating minimum required sample size

So how many limpets did we actually need to sample at each site to detect an ecologically important difference? We can calculate it using the power, significance level, and the estimated effect size. We'll use some rule of thumb values plugged into the formula - effect size of 0.8 (large effect), power of 0.8 and significance level of 0.05.

```{r}
pwr.t.test(
  n = NULL,
  d = 0.8,
  sig.level = 0.05,
  power = 0.80,
  type = "two.sample"
)

```

Could we really have measured only 25 limpets at each site and still detected an effect?

```{r}
# This code chooses 25 random observations from each site and creates a subsample data frame
Subsample <- All_Size_Data |>
   group_by(site) |>
 sample_n(25)

count(Subsample)

# because each subsample is random, you'll get a different p-value each time you run it. 
t.test(shell_length_mm ~ site, Subsample)
```

The fact that we have such a large data set actually gives us a good opportunity to demonstrate **sampling distributions.** *goes one level deeper into Inception*

We are PRETTY DARN CONFIDENT that our difference is real, right? If we sampled only 25 limpets from each site, how often would we detect that difference? Some samples by chance might be more similar, some less. This simulation subsamples from our data set 1000 times, then runs the t-test to see if the two random samples are different.

```{r}
pvals <- c()
diffs <- c()
for(i in 1:1000) {
  Subsample <- All_Size_Data |>
    group_by(site) |>
    sample_n(25)
  temp <- t.test(shell_length_mm ~ site, Subsample)
  diffs[i] <- temp$estimate[2] - temp$estimate[1]
  pvals[i] <- temp$p.value
}

temp <- tibble(diffs, pvals) |> 
  mutate(sig = case_when(
    pvals >= 0.05 ~ "NS",
    pvals < 0.05 & pvals >= 0.01 ~ "*",
    pvals < 0.01 & pvals >= 0.001 ~ "**",
    pvals < 0.001 ~ "***"
  )) 

temp |>
  group_by(sig) |>
  count()

temp2 <- temp |>
  group_by(sig) |>
  count() |>
  ggplot() + 
  aes(x = sig, y = n) + 
  geom_col()

temp2

```

Is a smaller sample more likely to pass the normality test? Does this change how we think about tests of normality for data sets with large sample sizes?

```{r}
full_model <- lm(shell_length_mm ~ site, All_Size_Data)

plot(full_model, which = 2)

shapiro.test(full_model$residuals)



subsample_model <- lm(shell_length_mm ~ site, Subsample)

plot(subsample_model, which = 2)

shapiro.test(subsample_model$residuals)
```

### Power

Power is one of the harder components to conceptualize and measure. Power is equal to **1 - Type II error probability** **(1 - β).** Type II error probability is the odds that you fail to reject the null hypothesis when it is actually false, that is, there is a difference, but you missed it. Therefore, power is the odds that you successfully find a true difference (e.g., true positive). This is also sometimes referred to as **sensitivity**.

How do we decide what acceptable power is for an experiment? A power of 0.8 is a conventional rule of thumb for experiments across many fields - that is, accepting a 20% chance that there is a difference, but your test failed to detect it (by chance, because sampling is random!).

#### Intuiting Power

In what kind of test might higher power be really important? Consider the following scenarios:

- Scientists develop a test for a new and scary viral infection that is nearly always deadly if untreated, but is very treatable with an inexpensive medication if caught early. You are exposed to this virus and your test is negative; however, the doctor tells you that 20% of the time an infected person takes this test, it has a false negative. How confident are you about going home without the medication?

  - Fun Fact! OTC COVID-19 rapid antigen tests have a sensitivity of about 0.65 in symptomatic individuals and about 0.44 in asymptomatic individuals (Jegerlehner et al. 2021, *Int.J.Inf.Dis.*). This is why most OTC test kits recommend taking two tests within 24 hours; the probability of getting a false negative twice in a row is much lower!

```{r}
(1 - 0.65)^2
```

- You are an EPA scientist tasked with determining whether a new fertilizer should be approved for use in agriculture near rivers; anecdotal evidence suggests that it may have detrimental impacts on river invertebrate communities. You are given unreplicated data from 8 rivers; four where the fertilizer is used, four where it is not. Assuming that a moderate effect size (0.5) would be important and α = 0.05, how confident would you be approving or rejecting the fertilizer for use based on the river data?

```{r}
Power_Fert <- pwr.t.test(
  n = 4,
  d = 0.5,
  sig.level = 0.05,
  power = NULL,
  type = "two.sample"
)

Power_Fert$power
```

Not very confident! With that low sample size, if you decide that there is no difference (i.e., that it is safe to use the fertilizer) the odds that you are correct is less than 10%. The right thing to do here would be to delay a decision until you have gathered more data on the safety of this fertilizer.

#### Power and Sample Size

When we calculated our minimum sample size for our owl limpet study earlier, we used the conventional (and pretty arbitrary) power level of 0.8. Perhaps we are not satisfied with that low of power and want to have higher confidence in our findings.

How much does raising the power we desire increase our minimum sample size?

```{r}
Power08 <- pwr.t.test(
  n = NULL,
  d = 0.8,
  sig.level = ,
  power = 0.8,
  type = "two.sample"
)

Power08
```

```{r}
Power09 <- pwr.t.test(
  n = NULL,
  d = 0.8,
  sig.level = 0.05,
  power = 0.90,
  type = "two.sample"
)

Power095 <- pwr.t.test(
  n = NULL,
  d = 0.8,
  sig.level = 0.05,
  power = 0.95,
  type = "two.sample"
)

Power099 <- pwr.t.test(
  n = NULL,
  d = 0.8,
  sig.level = 0.05,
  power = 0.99,
  type = "two.sample"
)

Power0999 <- pwr.t.test(
  n = NULL,
  d = 0.8,
  sig.level = 0.05,
  power = 0.999,
  type = "two.sample"
)

Power09$n
Power095$n
Power099$n
Power0999$n
```

What was the **power** of our full-scale owl limpet study for the difference between CDM and TC?

```{r}
pwr.t.test(
  n = 187,
  d = 0.9599906,
  sig.level = 0.05,
  power = NULL,
  type = "two.sample"
)

# our experiment was so overpowered that R just rounded it to 1. 

```

### Significance

Referring back to Table 1, you may recall that Type I Error (α) is the odds of getting a false positive. Across lots of scientific fields, this value is conventionally set at 0.05.

Remember our subsampling exercise before - some proportion of the time, the random sub-sample of the data was just randomly a lot of weird values and the test failed to detect the difference. This is conceptually similar; in practice, this is the likelihood, given that the null hypothesis is true, that the data you observed (sampled) occurred by chance. If your data are all pretty close to the values predicted by the null hypothesis, that likelihood is high. If your data are further away from the values predicted under the null, the likelihood is smaller.

#### Intuiting significance

It is important to note that significance is a threshold; above a certain value, you fail to reject the null, but below it, you do reject the null.

- Increasing significance (i.e., raising from 0.05 to 0.1) means accepting a higher likelihood that you will have a false positive, which weakens the conclusions that you can make from your experiment.

- Lowering significance (i.e., lowering from 0.05 to 0.01) means your test is more conservative and very unlikely to have a false positive, but you may miss some true effects, depending on your sample size and other factors.

#### Trade-off with power

There is a trade-off here with power! Adjusting your significance lower (i.e., reducing the odds that you got the distribution by chance) it raises the bar for how different your samples have to be in order to reject the null hypothesis; with the same exact sample, you are less likely to reject the null, which correspondingly means you are **less likely to [correctly]{.underline} reject the null**.

![](https://www.scribbr.com/wp-content/uploads/2021/01/type-i-and-type-ii-error.png){width="500"}

Let's play around with this concept. What if we hold the effect size constant, and vary sample size, significance, and see what happens to power? Remember, our optimal place is where significance is low as possible and power is as high as possible.

```{r}
n_test <- c(rep(10, 10), rep(25, 10), rep(40, 10), rep(80, 10))
d_test <- rep(0.5, 40)
sig_level <- rep(c(0.0001, 0.0005, 0.001, 0.005, 0.01, 0.05, 0.1, 0.15, 0.2, 0.25), 4)

test <- tibble(n_test, d_test, sig_level) |>
  mutate(power = pwr.t.test(
    n = n_test, 
    d = d_test, 
    sig.level = sig_level, 
    type = "two.sample")$power)

ggplot(test) +
  aes(x = sig_level, y = power, color = factor(n_test), group = factor(n_test)) + 
  geom_point() +
  geom_line()
```

Where do you get the most "bang" (power) for your "buck" (low significance) when the sample size is small?

- the steepest part of the curve for sample sizes under 50 or so is usually between 0.01 and 0.05 - gains in power reduce after that.

Where do you get the most "bang" (power) for your "buck" (low significance) when the sample size is large?

- With a large sample size, the gains in power don't level off until after \~ 0.01. A lower significance level may be appropriate for larger sample sizes to maximize power.

What was the minimum sample size needed to detect the difference between TC near vs far?

```{r}
t.test(shell_length_mm ~ location, data = TC_Data2023)
d_tc <- abs(43.92547 - 42.29670)/sd(TC_Data2023$shell_length_mm)

pwr.t.test(
  n = NULL,
  d = d_tc,
  sig.level = 0.05,
  power = 0.8,
  type = "two.sample"
)


```

What was the minimum sample size needed to detect the difference between CDM near vs far with a power of 0.8?

```{r}
cdm_test <- t.test(shell_length_mm ~ location, data = CDM_Data2022)
d_cdm <- abs(cdm_test$estimate[1] - cdm_test$estimate[2])/sd(CDM_Data2022$shell_length_mm)

pwr.t.test(
  n = NULL,
  d = d_cdm,
  sig.level = 0.05,
  power = 0.8,
  type = "two.sample"
)

```
